maybe figured out the issue.
if we shift left 26 then subtract 1, what happens is it shifts too far left it goes off bounds and becomes 00000,
then when subtracting 1 instead of making it 11111, it becomes 10000 signed.. ?? maybe?? not really. let's run through it.

rbx = r11 = 0
rcx = r14 = 25
rbx = 0 ; (shr 6)
rcx = 0 ; (shr 6)
jmp do_it


r12 = r11 = 0
r12 = 0 ; (shr 6 shl 6)
rbx = 0 ; (subtract base index)
rcx = 25 ; (subtract base index)
r12 = 0 ; (shr 6, make it segment)
r15 = rcx = 25

r10 = 1 ; THE bitmap
rcx -= rbx ; rcx = 25
rcx += 1 ; rcx = 26
shl r10, cl (26)
; r10 = 0000000000000000000000000000000000000100000000000000000000000000
sub r10, 1
; r10 = 0000000000000000000000000000000000000011111111111111111111111111
mov rcx, 127
sub rcx, r15
; rcx = 127 - 25 = 122
shl r10, cl (122)

should be 63, not 127.
retry with 63.
mov rcx, 63
sub rcx, r15
; rcx = 63 - 25 = 38
shl r10, cl (38)
; r10 = 1111111111111111111111111100000000000000000000000000000000000000
; good. what if we tried to fill all 64 though?


rbx = r11 = 0
rcx = r14 = 63
rbx = 0 ; (shr 6)
rcx = 0 ; (shr 6)
jmp do_it

r12 = r11 = 0

that's not correct. the 1s only started appearing at index 65 and ended at index 127.

ok, the issue was due to shl r10 (1), 64 keeping r10 as 1 when it shouldve become 0.
    basically there is a case where we want to fill all 64 bits, so we shift left just 1 bit over the highest, so when we subtract 1 all bits are filled.
    in this rare case, it didn't make it all 0 when it should've, so that when subtracting you get all 1 bits as desired.
fixed it with a workaround, but now there's an EXCEPTION_PRIV_INSTRUCTION.
we should step through in x64dbg to find where the issue is.


why did it hit x0_left twice?
ok, the loop index (r11 and r14) are necessary to be saved when calling itself in the recursion, but they get changed every call.
maybe we add some push/pop, but i really don't want to access the memory at all. i should rewrite this subroutine.

now im wondering how the rust code even works, when i did (1u128 << 128) - 1. why did it work perfectly and make 111111... ?

i think i realize why the CNT0 and CNT1 for "a" are not 1s.
i think for "aahed" it goes backwards, so writes the 1s for "d", "e", "h", "a". but then when it does "a" again, the XOR makes them 0 again.
we only want to loop through the unique letters of the word, not the same letters twice. the reason it works in the rust code is we were using OR, not XOR.

ok, ill make write_raw_bit do OR and keep write_raw_bit_sequence as XOR.
then, we'll switch the order for writing 'positions' for green (OR then XOR), and we get

what is the correct bitmask?

10000000000000000000000000

10011001000000000000000000
10011001000000000000000000
10011001000000000000000000
10011001000000000000000000

so it seems, if we see a gray letter, we are blocking CNT0 and keeping all the other CNTs as 0.
instead, we should block all CNT except CNT0.
and, when we saw a green + gray letter, we blocked CNT0 and CNT1, but we actually shouldve blocked CNT0, CNT2, CNT3, CNT4, CNT5
